text:
Every recursive resolver keeps the answers it receives and reuses them. Each record carries a TTL, a 32-bit counter of seconds defined in RFC 1035. The TTL lets the resolver reuse an answer without asking the authoritative server again.

Say you change an A record at noon, and its TTL is 3600 seconds. A resolver that looked up the record at 11:59 will keep returning the old IP address until nearly 1 p.m. Clients have no reason to doubt the address, because nothing marks it as stale. So propagation speed depends on when the resolver's cache expires, not on when you made the edit.

Failed lookups are cached too. Suppose a resolver cached NXDOMAIN before your new subdomain existed. Under RFC 2308 negative caching, it will keep saying the subdomain doesn't exist until the SOA minimum runs out.

Browsers and OS stub resolvers add their own private caches on top, and some ignore TTLs entirely.

I call this TTL debt. Operators have to plan around migrations by lowering TTLs to 300 seconds, starting one full old-TTL period beforehand. Otherwise the internet keeps navigating by an outdated map.
